authors: Noy, S.; Zhang, W. (Shakked Noy, Whitney Zhang)
title: Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence
note: All bibliographic fields verified as given. Author list and order (Noy, then Zhang) match across publisher, PubMed, SSRN and Semantic Scholar records. Title wording exact, including lowercase style. Substantive claims in the original note also check out against the published abstract: 453 college-educated professionals, incentivized occupation-specific writing tasks, average time taken down 40%, output quality up 18%, inequality between workers decreased. The claim that ChatGPT 'mostly substitutes for worker effort rather than complementing worker skills' is the authors' own framing, so the note's use of it is fair.
evidence: Search for the exact quoted title plus both surnames plus the journal returned mutually independent records agreeing on every field: (1) publisher page science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adh2586; (2) PubMed record pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37440646/; (3) Semantic Scholar paper record (corpus 8d020275181c69e5e768c6ffc40e09710a6f54f1); (4) SSRN working-paper precursor abstract_id=4375283 (Shakked Noy, Whitney Zhang) confirming full given names and order; (5) MIT Economics author-hosted PDF economics.mit.edu/sites/default/files/inline-files/Noy_Zhang_1.pdf. Volume 381, issue 6654, pages 187-192, July 2023 are consistent across the publisher and indexing records.

authors: Brynjolfsson, E.; Li, D.; Raymond, L. (Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey Raymond)
title: Generative AI at Work
note: BIBLIOGRAPHIC METADATA IS FULLY CORRECT AS SUBMITTED — authors, order, title, journal, 140(2):889-942, 2025, DOI 10.1093/qje/qjae044 all verified. The CORRECTED verdict applies to the descriptive note, which reports figures from an earlier NBER working-paper draft rather than the published QJE version. TRUE published values: the sample is 5,172 customer-support agents (NOT 5,179), and average productivity measured as issues resolved per hour rose 15% (NOT 14%). Also correct the characterisation of the high-skill result: the published paper states that less experienced and lower-skilled workers improved both speed and quality, while the most experienced and highest-skilled workers saw small gains in speed AND SMALL DECLINES IN QUALITY — this is stronger than the note's 'minimal effect on experienced high-skilled workers' and materially strengthens the pipeline-erosion argument the note wants to make. The '34% for novice and low-skilled workers' figure should be re-checked against the published text before use, as it too may derive from the working-paper draft. The published abstract also supports the note's learning mechanism: AI assistance facilitated worker learning and improved English fluency, particularly among international agents.
evidence: Search for the exact quoted title plus all three surnames plus journal and volume returned independent agreeing records: (1) Oxford Academic article page academic.oup.com/qje/article/140/2/889/7990658; (2) RePEc/IDEAS handle ideas.repec.org/a/oup/qjecon/v140y2025i2p889-942..html, which independently encodes volume 140, issue 2, pages 889-942, 2025; (3) Stanford GSB faculty publications record listing it as a journal article; (4) author-hosted PDF danielle.li/assets/docs/GenerativeAIatWork.pdf; (5) NBER Working Paper w31161 as the precursor. The corrected sample size and effect size come from the published abstract text surfaced in the search ('data from 5,172 customer-support agents', 'by 15% on average'), which conflicts with the 5,179/14% figures in the submitted note; those latter figures match the earlier NBER draft.

authors: Dell'Acqua, F.; McFowland, E., III; Mollick, E.R.; Lifshitz-Assaf, H.; Kellogg, K.C.; Rajendran, S.; Krayer, L.; Candelon, F.; Lakhani, K.R.
title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
note: Journal version verified: Organization Science 37(2):403-423, 2026, DOI 10.1287/orsc.2025.21838. Nine-author list and order confirmed exactly as submitted. One name note: the fourth author is indexed as Hila Lifshitz-Assaf on SSRN and in the working-paper lineage; the submitted record's remark that the published version shortens this to 'Hila Lifshitz' is plausible but was NOT independently confirmed from the publisher record in this session — use 'Lifshitz-Assaf, H.' unless you can check the published byline directly, since that is the form both indexing records show. Substantive claims verified against the abstract: preregistered experiment, 758 consultants at BCG, three arms (no AI, GPT-4, GPT-4 plus prompt-engineering overview); inside the frontier, tasks completed +12.2%, quality +40% (the abstract's 'more than 40%' phrasing is commonly reported; the note's 'over 30%' is a safe understatement), time roughly -25%; outside the frontier, correctness fell 19 percentage points. The submitted note's guidance to prefer the journal version over HBS Working Paper 24-013 is sound.

authors: Peng, S.; Kalliamvakou, E.; Cihon, P.; Demirer, M.
title: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
note: Controlled experiment in which recruited developers implemented an HTTP server in JavaScript; the Copilot treatment group finished 55.8% faster than controls. Heterogeneity analysis is the relevant part for this slot: less experienced developers showed both higher adoption and larger productivity gains, and the authors argue AI pair programmers could ease entry into software careers. Useful as the software-engineering instance of the experience gradient, and as a counterpoint the model can test -- easier entry into the occupation does not by itself guarantee the accumulation of expertise that senior roles require. CAVEAT: this remains a non-peer-reviewed preprint as of July 2026; no journal version was found. Flag it as a working paper in the manuscript rather than presenting it as refereed.
evidence: Confirmed independently by (1) arXiv abstract page arxiv.org/abs/2302.06590 (submitted 13 February 2023); (2) Semantic Scholar record (corpus ID 8d02.../15abedb...); (3) dblp record journals/corr/abs-2302-06590; (4) Microsoft Research publications page; (5) NASA ADS bibcode 2023arXiv230206590P. Author list and order identical across all five. Extensive search for a peer-reviewed journal or conference version returned none, so the arXiv preprint is the citable version.

authors: Brynjolfsson, E.; Chandar, B.; Chen, R.
title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
journal: Stanford Digital Economy Lab Working Paper, Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (SIEPR), Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
note: The anchor empirical result for the slot. Uses high-frequency individual-level ADP payroll microdata (largest U.S. payroll provider) to show a ~13 percent relative employment decline (~16 percent when controlling for firm-level shocks) for workers aged 22-25 in the most AI-exposed occupations since late 2022, while employment of experienced workers in the same occupations was stable or growing. Adjustment runs through headcount rather than wages, and is concentrated where AI automates rather than augments. Directly supplies the empirical premise that generative AI bites at the entry level first, i.e. exactly the pipeline stage the system dynamics model targets. First circulated August 2025 (dated 26 August 2025), revised November 2025 (13 November 2025); still a working paper as of mid-2026, no journal version confirmed and no NBER number found. No numbered series identifier was displayed on the SIEPR or Digital Economy Lab landing pages, so volume/issue left blank rather than guessed.
evidence: Confirmed independently by: (1) Stanford Digital Economy Lab publication page (digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/publication/canaries-in-the-coal-mine-...); (2) SIEPR working paper page (siepr.stanford.edu/publications/working-paper/canaries-coal-mine-six-facts-about-recent-employment-effects-artificial); (3) two hosted PDFs of the paper itself (digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Canaries_BrynjolfssonChandarChen.pdf and .../app/uploads/2025/11/CanariesintheCoalMine_Nov25.pdf); (4) third-party redistributions of the draft by University of Chicago CEHD, AAAS, World Bank and Bank of England seminar materials; (5) Erik Brynjolfsson's own research page (brynjolfsson.com/research). Explicitly checked NBER and RePEc/IDEAS: no NBER working paper number or RePEc handle surfaced, so none is asserted.

title: Generative AI as Seniority-Biased Technological Change: Evidence from U.S. Résumé and Job Posting Data
journal: SSRN Working Paper No. 5425555, Social Science Research Network, Rochester, NY, USA
note: Firm-level counterpart to Brynjolfsson et al. and the cleanest evidence that the mechanism is a hiring-flow shutdown rather than a firing shock. Uses U.S. résumé data on roughly 62 million workers across ~285,000 firms (2015-2025), identifying generative AI adoption from text analysis of job postings for dedicated 'GenAI integrator' roles. After adoption, junior employment falls sharply at adopting firms relative to non-adopters while senior employment is essentially unchanged; the decline concentrates in the most GenAI-exposed occupations and is driven by slower hiring, not by higher separations or faster promotions. Coins 'seniority-biased technological change', which is a directly usable framing for the model's inflow-to-the-junior-stock variable. Dated 31 August 2025; authors affiliated with Harvard. Note the first author's full surname is the compound 'Hosseini Maasoum' (often shortened to 'Hosseini' in press coverage).
evidence: Confirmed independently by: (1) SSRN abstract page, abstract_id=5425555, and its registered DOI resolver link doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5425555; (2) ResearchGate record (publication 395371355) with matching title and both authors; (3) Stanford Digital Economy Lab seminar listing and Stanford events calendar for a 22 September 2025 talk of the same title by Seyed M. Hosseini and Guy Lichtinger; (4) SSRN's own announcement of the paper; (5) independent press coverage of the findings in Forbes and MIT Technology Review, plus mirrored copies of the PDF on third-party sites.

title: Automation, AI, and the Intergenerational Transmission of Knowledge
journal: Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) Discussion Paper No. DP20940, London, UK
note: The theoretical backbone for the paper's central causal story: automating entry-level tasks severs the channel through which tacit, hard-to-codify knowledge passes from experts to novices. Builds a model in which the competitive equilibrium features socially excessive automation of early-career work, because experts cannot be compensated for the knowledge novices absorb from them. Generates an explicit intergenerational trade-off: entry-level automation raises output on adoption but can lower long-run growth and welfare even when entry-level employment does not fall, by reallocating novices away from the most productive experts. Calibrated magnitudes are directly usable as system dynamics parameters: automating 5 percent of entry-level tasks cuts long-run U.S. output growth by about 0.05 percentage points per year, and 30 percent automation slows growth by more than 0.3 points. Also circulated as arXiv preprint 2507.16078 (first posted 21 July 2025, v9 revised 8 June 2026) and as SSRN Working Paper No. 5360803; the CEPR Discussion Paper (dated 9 June 2026) is the most formal series designation. Author at IESE Business School, University of Navarra.
evidence: Confirmed independently by: (1) CEPR discussion paper landing page cepr.org/publications/dp20940 and CEPR's own new-paper announcement naming DP20940 and the author; (2) arXiv abstract page arxiv.org/abs/2507.16078 plus the full-text HTML v9; (3) RePEc/IDEAS handle ideas.repec.org/p/arx/papers/2507.16078.html; (4) SSRN abstract page abstract_id=5360803; (5) NASA ADS record 2025arXiv250716078I; (6) ResearchGate record 393923538 and the author's own site enriqueide.com. Multiple sources agree on sole authorship.

title: Looking for the Ladder: Is AI Impacting Entry-Level Jobs?
journal: The American Worker Project, Economic Innovation Group, Washington, DC, USA
note: The best-documented skeptical counterweight in this literature, and worth citing so the model's assumptions are not stated as settled fact. Analysing U.S. job postings, the authors find that vacancies did fall more in AI-exposed occupations, but that the decline began around mid-2022, roughly six months before the public release of ChatGPT in November 2022, and that postings for junior roles subsequently stabilised faster than senior ones. They attribute the pattern to the sharpest monetary tightening cycle in four decades rather than to technological displacement. Useful for a sensitivity/identification discussion: it defines the confounder (interest-rate-driven demand shock) that any entry-level AI displacement claim must survive, and the Stanford Digital Economy Lab published a direct response on interest rates and timing. Published 14 January 2026 as part of EIG's American Worker Project. Authors are, respectively, AI and Economy Lead and Chief Economist at Google, which is a disclosure worth noting in text. Second author's surname is the compound 'Curto Millet' (rendered 'Millet' in EIG's filename).
evidence: Confirmed independently by: (1) the report PDF hosted on the publisher's own domain, eig.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/TAWP-Iscenko-Millet.pdf; (2) EIG's Agglomerations publication post 'Looking for the Ladder' and EIG's January 2026 monthly highlights post, both giving the 14 January 2026 date and both author names in full; (3) independent citation and summary of the findings in Brookings / The Hamilton Project and PIIE commentary pieces reviewing AI labor-market research; (4) SIEPR's policy brief and the Stanford Digital Economy Lab's rebuttal note, which engage with the interest-rate timing argument. No DOI is issued for EIG reports, so the field is left empty.

title: Industrial Dynamics
note: The founding text of system dynamics: establishes feedback-loop structure, stocks and flows, and delays as the determinants of system behavior, and argues that counterintuitive dynamics arise from structure rather than external shocks. Anchors the methodological claim that a pipeline-erosion model should be built from endogenous feedback structure rather than exogenous trend extrapolation.
evidence: MIT ArchivesSpace digital object record for Forrester's 'Industrial Dynamics'; WorldCat catalog record OCLC 254933; AbeBooks listing under ISBN 0-262-06003-5 / 9780262060035. Publisher (MIT Press, Cambridge, MA), year 1961, and 464-page extent agree across all three. Note: 1999 Pegasus Communications reprint has 479 pp., so pagination differs by edition.

title: Business Dynamics: Systems Thinking and Modeling for a Complex World
note: The standard graduate textbook and practitioner reference for system dynamics modeling: causal loop and stock-and-flow diagramming, formulation of rate equations, aging chains and co-flows, delay structures, and the full battery of model-testing procedures. Directly supplies the aging-chain/co-flow formalism used to represent junior-to-experienced worker progression, plus the validation test suite (extreme conditions, dimensional consistency, behavior reproduction, sensitivity).
evidence: WorldCat catalog record OCLC 42771322 (Irwin/McGraw-Hill, Boston, 2000); McGraw-Hill Education higher-ed product page; Open Library record OL14752748M; System Dynamics Society book listing. ISBN 0-07-231135-5; extent xxvi + 982 pp. consistent across catalog records.

title: Formal aspects of model validity and validation in system dynamics
note: The canonical statement of validation practice for causal-descriptive (white-box) system dynamics models, distinguishing structure validity from behavior validity and presenting a taxonomy of formal tests in sequence: direct structure tests, structure-oriented behavior tests, then behavior pattern tests. Provides the methodological justification for validating a policy model on structural plausibility and behavior-pattern fit rather than point-prediction accuracy.
evidence: Wiley Online Library article landing page (System Dynamics Review 12(3), 183-210, DOI resolves); Semantic Scholar paper record; SCIRP reference index entry. Volume 12, issue 3, and page range 183-210 agree across all three.

title: All models are wrong: reflections on becoming a systems scientist
note: Text of the Jay W. Forrester Award address at the 2002 International System Dynamics Conference. Argues that all models are necessarily wrong and that their value lies in disciplined use under explicit boundary assumptions, that misperceptions of feedback and delays make dynamic systems systematically counterintuitive, and that modeling must be paired with client engagement to change mental models. Supports framing model results as policy insight about feedback structure rather than point forecasts of AI-driven labor displacement.
evidence: Wiley Online Library article landing page (DOI 10.1002/sdr.261); author's own PDF hosted at web.mit.edu/jsterman/www/All_Models_Are_Wrong_(SDR).pdf; Semantic Scholar record; SCIRP reference index. Volume 18, issue 4, and page range 501-531 agree across sources.

authors: Eloundou, T.; Manning, S.; Mishkin, P.; Rock, D.
title: GPTs are GPTs: Labor market impact potential of LLMs
note: Builds an O*NET task-level rubric (human + GPT-4 labels) for LLM exposure and estimates that ~80% of US workers have at least 10% of tasks exposed and ~19% have at least 50% exposed, with exposure rising with wage and educational attainment; the canonical source for parameterising task-level GenAI exposure of entry-level versus experienced roles.
evidence: Confirmed independently by the Science publisher page (science.org DOI 10.1126/science.adj0998), the NASA ADS record with bibcode 2024Sci...384.1306E giving volume 384 page 1306, and Semantic Scholar / arXiv 2303.10130 / IDEAS-RePEc records for the underlying preprint.

title: The Race between Man and Machine: Implications of Technology for Growth, Factor Shares, and Employment
note: The seminal task-based framework in which automation displaces labour from existing tasks while the creation of new tasks reinstates it, with endogenous capital accumulation and directed technical change; supplies the displacement/reinstatement structure that a system dynamics model of pipeline erosion can formalise as competing stocks and flows.
evidence: Confirmed independently by the American Economic Association article page (aeaweb.org, DOI 10.1257/aer.20160696), the MIT DSpace repository record, the Yale/Cowles CFP-1884 journal-publication listing, and NBER Working Paper 22252 as the precursor.

authors: Albanesi, S.; Dias da Silva, A.; Jimeno, J.F.; Lamo, A.; Wabitsch, A.
title: New technologies and jobs in Europe
note: Measures occupational AI exposure at the three-digit occupation level across 16 European countries (2011-2019) and finds employment shares rose on average in more AI-exposed occupations, especially those with higher proportions of young and skilled workers, with heterogeneity tied to technology diffusion, education, product market regulation and employment protection; a recent economics-journal counterweight to pure displacement narratives and a source of policy levers for the model.
evidence: Confirmed independently by the Oxford Academic Economic Policy article page (academic.oup.com, DOI 10.1093/epolic/eiae058, vol. 40, no. 121, pp. 71-139), the IDEAS-RePEc record oup/ecpoli/v40y2025i121p71-139, the Economic Policy journal proof PDF at economic-policy.org, and NBER Working Paper 31357 / IZA DP 16227 as the working-paper versions.

title: Capability Traps and Self-Confirming Attribution Errors in the Dynamics of Process Improvement
note: Seminal system dynamics account of the capability trap: delays between investing in improvement and reaping its rewards, combined with self-confirming attribution errors, push organizations to keep 'working harder' rather than 'working smarter', eroding the very capability that would relieve the pressure. Directly transferable to a pipeline model where firms substitute AI for entry-level hiring under short-run pressure and thereby erode the stock of experienced workers.
evidence: SAGE Journals publisher page (journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.2307/3094806); Semantic Scholar record (paper b64a02437cc1...); SciRP reference index giving ASQ 47, 265-295; DeepDyve ASQ 2002 v47/i2 issue listing confirming issue 2; SSRN working-paper record (abstract_id=320380).

title: Nobody Ever Gets Credit for Fixing Problems That Never Happened: Creating and Sustaining Process Improvement
note: Managerial-facing statement of the same reinforcing structure: because prevention is invisible in the metrics while firefighting is rewarded, improvement effort is systematically underfunded and the organization settles into a low-capability equilibrium. Provides the attribution/reward-asymmetry argument for why firms will not voluntarily fund junior-worker development whose payoff is delayed and diffuse.
evidence: SAGE Journals publisher page (journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.2307/41166101); author's own PDF at web.mit.edu/nelsonr/www/Repenning=Sterman_CMR_su01_.pdf whose running head reads 'CALIFORNIA MANAGEMENT REVIEW VOL. 43, NO. 4 SUMMER 2001 64'; Harvard Business Review store listing (product CMR208); SciRP reference index giving CMR 43, 64-88; Semantic Scholar record.

title: Capability Erosion Dynamics
note: Simulation-based theory of how strategically relevant capabilities are lost, not just built. Identifies the 'adaptation trap': managers searching locally for the best workload level systematically overload the organization, and because capability erodes with a long delay the local search never reveals the damage. Supplies the erosion-side stock-and-flow logic and the delayed-feedback mechanism for the paper's junior-to-experienced conversion pipeline.
evidence: Wiley Online Library publisher page (sms.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/smj.2354); MIT DSpace repository record hdl.handle.net/1721.1/111119; Semantic Scholar record (paper 055ed8106dbc...); MIT Sloan publication document listing; Hazhir Rahmandad's MIT Sloan CV.

title: Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System
note: The canonical hierarchy of twelve leverage points, ranked from weakest (constants, parameters, subsidies, taxes, standards) to strongest (the goals of the system, the mindset/paradigm out of which the system arises, and the power to transcend paradigms). Directly justifies the paper's argument that subsidizing junior hiring or tweaking training budgets are low-order parameter interventions, whereas changing the goal of the firm's staffing function (from short-run cost minimization to pipeline sustainment) or the shared paradigm that entry-level work is a cost centre rather than the production function for experienced workers are high-order leverage points. Also the origin of the 'counterintuitive / push the wrong way' observation used to frame policy resistance in the model.
evidence: Confirmed independently by: (1) the authoritative full text hosted by The Donella Meadows Project at donellameadows.org (Leverage_Points.pdf, plus the archive page 'Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System'); (2) a university repository copy in the NCEAS Sustainability Science working-group reading list (groups.nceas.ucsb.edu), cited as 'Meadows, D. 1999. Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System. Hartland, VT: Sustainability Institute'; (3) an Open Library catalogue record and multiple Scientific Research Publishing reference records giving the same author/title/year/publisher. Publisher location Hartland, Vermont, USA. NOTE: page count deliberately left blank — sources disagree (some reference databases say 10 p., the circulating PDF runs longer), and I would not guess. The essay is an expanded version of a shorter piece that appeared in Whole Earth, Winter 1997.

title: Thinking in Systems: A Primer
note: The standard primer on stock-and-flow reasoning, delays, balancing and reinforcing feedback, and — most relevant here — the chapter material on 'system traps' and why systems resist policy. Supplies the paper's vocabulary for policy resistance (bounded rationality of each actor, drift to low performance, eroding goals, seeking the wrong goal, shifting the burden to the intervenor), each of which maps onto a failure mode of the junior-to-senior conversion pipeline: firms rationally cut entry-level hiring, the industry's implicit standard for 'enough experienced staff' erodes, and reliance on generative AI shifts the burden away from human skill formation. Also restates the leverage-points hierarchy in book form, making it the citable source when the 1999 working paper is considered too grey. Edited posthumously by Diana Wright of the Sustainability Institute after Meadows' death in 2001.
evidence: Confirmed independently by: (1) WorldCat catalogue record 'Thinking in systems : a primer' (OCLC 225871309); (2) the Wikipedia article 'Thinking In Systems: A Primer' giving Chelsea Green Publishing, 2008, 240 pp., ISBN 978-1-60358-055-7 and naming Diana Wright as editor; (3) the System Dynamics Society's own product page for the title; (4) publisher-derived retail listings (ISBN 9781603580557) and Goodreads editions data. Publisher location: White River Junction, Vermont, USA. Page count 240 reflects the widely listed Chelsea Green edition; some printings are listed at 218 pp., so treat the figure as edition-dependent if MDPI requires it.

authors: Ghaffarzadegan, N.; Lyneis, J.; Richardson, G.P.
title: How small system dynamics models can help the public policy process
note: Argues that public policy fails because of complexity in both the system and the policy-making process, and that small, transparent system dynamics models — rather than large detailed ones — are what actually move policy debate, because they are communicable, expose the endogenous feedback structure, and produce a few memorable counterintuitive insights. Demonstrated with two worked cases, one in urban planning and one in social welfare. This is the direct methodological warrant for the paper's modelling choice: a deliberately small, aggregate model of the entry-level-to-experienced conversion pipeline is defensible precisely because its purpose is policy insight and counterintuitive-behaviour diagnosis, not point forecasting of labour-market quantities. Recognised as one of the most influential articles published in System Dynamics Review.
evidence: Confirmed independently by: (1) Wiley Online Library article page for doi 10.1002/sdr.442, System Dynamics Review, Ghaffarzadegan 2011; (2) Semantic Scholar record for the same paper (author string Ghaffarzadegan-Lyneis); (3) a Google Scholar citation-lookup record explicitly encoding volume=27, pages=22-44, publication_year=2011, journal=Syst. Dyn. Rev., authors GP Richardson, J Lyneis, N Ghaffarzadegan; (4) ResearchGate publication 227664100. Volume 27, issue 1, pp. 22-44 corroborated across the Wiley listing and the Scholar metadata; full journal name is System Dynamics Review (published for the System Dynamics Society).

authors: Willis, G.; Cave, S.; Kunc, M.
title: Strategic workforce planning in healthcare: A multi-methodology approach
note: Presents the Robust Workforce Planning Framework used by the UK Centre for Workforce Intelligence, combining system dynamics stock-and-flow modelling of the training-to-practice human resource chain with scenario/horizon-scanning methods for national-level workforce policy; the canonical OR reference for SD-based workforce pipeline modelling and directly supports modelling training and experience-accumulation delays.
evidence: ScienceDirect publisher page (PII S0377221717310196); RePEc/IDEAS record eee:ejores:v:267:y:2018:i:1:p:250-263; University of Warwick WRAP institutional repository (eprint 95601) — all three give volume 267, issue 1, pp. 250-263, DOI 10.1016/j.ejor.2017.11.008

authors: Leerapan, B.; Teekasap, P.; Urwannachotima, N.; Jaichuen, W.; Chiangchaisakulthai, K.; Udomaksorn, K.; Meeyai, A.; Noree, T.; Sawaengdee, K.
title: System dynamics modelling of health workforce planning to address future challenges of Thailand's Universal Health Coverage
note: Group-model-building plus stock-and-flow simulation of health workforce supply and demand over 2018-2037; shows a reinforcing 'vicious cycle' in which rising hospital utilisation perpetuates chronic provider shortage, and tests policy leverage points. A template for combining participatory causal loop diagramming with SD policy testing on a human resource chain.

authors: Hynes, T.; Caulfield, P.; O'Connor, P.; Cullinan, J.
title: Self-sufficiency in the healthcare workforce: a system dynamics model of the domestic and foreign educated nursing and midwifery workforce in Ireland
note: Recent (Aug 2025) SD model tracking domestic versus foreign-educated nursing/midwifery stocks by age and gender, using regulator data to back out the student intake needed to reach self-sufficiency under alternative reform scenarios; quantifies the long pipeline lag between education places and practising workforce (e.g. 2021 recruitment need implied 3,965 student places back in 2017 versus 1,570 actually available).

title: System Dynamic Modeling to Study the Impact of Construction Industry Characteristics and Associated Macroeconomic Indicators on Workforce Size and Labor Retention Rate
journal: Journal of Construction Engineering and Management
note: SD model of the skilled-labour market built from three coupled subsystems (construction labour market, industry characteristics, economic conditions) that endogenises workforce size and retention rate; useful non-healthcare evidence that skill shortages arise from feedback between entry, retention and demand rather than from exogenous shocks.
evidence: ASCE Library publisher page (Journal of Construction Engineering and Management, Vol. 149, No. 10, DOI 10.1061/JCEMD4.COENG-13410); Missouri S&T Scholars' Mine institutional repository record civarc_enveng_facwork/2631; Dr. Islam H. El-adaway's Missouri S&T faculty publications list — consistent on authors, volume/issue and article number 04023100

title: The Economic Implications of Learning by Doing
note: Seminal formalization of learning-by-doing: productivity rises as a power function of cumulative experience (cumulative gross investment as the experience index), and because learning spills over to later entrants the competitive rate of investment/experience accumulation is below the social optimum. This is the canonical foundation for the learning-curve formulation of a stock-and-flow experience accumulation structure, and its externality argument directly supports the paper's claim that firms individually under-invest in the junior pipeline.
evidence: Oxford Academic / Review of Economic Studies article page (restud/article-abstract/29/3/155) giving vol. 29, issue 3, pp. 155-173; independently corroborated by SciRP reference record (29, 155-173), Semantic Scholar record, and a full-text PDF hosted by Haverford College. DOI 10.2307/2295952 shown on the OUP listing.

authors: Ericsson, K.A.; Krampe, R.T.; Tesch-Römer, C.
title: The Role of Deliberate Practice in the Acquisition of Expert Performance
note: Classic statement that expert-level performance is the product of prolonged, effortful, feedback-rich deliberate practice rather than innate talent; the violinist studies tie attained skill level to accumulated practice hours and establish the multi-year timescale of proficiency acquisition. Justifies a long, non-compressible time-to-proficiency delay in the model and, critically, the requirement of task exposure plus expert feedback — the two inputs that entry-level AI substitution removes.
evidence: PhilPapers and Semantic Scholar records both resolve DOI 10.1037/0033-295X.100.3.363 to Psychological Review 100(3), 363-406, 1993; independently corroborated by two separate SciRP reference records (Psychological Review, 100, 363-406) and by the Royal Society Open Science 25-year replication/re-examination article (Macnamara & Maitra, 2019) which cites the same volume and pages.

authors: Jarosch, G.; Oberfield, E.; Rossi-Hansberg, E.
title: Learning From Coworkers
note: Structural estimation on German administrative data showing that workers accumulate human capital by working alongside more knowledgeable coworkers: exposure to higher-skilled colleagues raises subsequent wage growth, and the estimated learning externality is economically large. Provides the empirical magnitude for the senior-to-junior knowledge-transfer flow in the model and shows the mechanism operates through ordinary co-working, not formal training — so thinning the junior cohort's contact with seniors degrades the transfer rate.
evidence: IDEAS/RePEc record (wly/emetrp/v89y2021i2p647-676) giving vol. 89, issue 2, pp. 647-676; independently corroborated by the Econometric Society's own article page (Econometrica vol. 89 issue 2, March 2021) and the Wiley Online Library entry carrying DOI 10.3982/ECTA16915. Working-paper version is NBER w25418.

authors: Emanuel, N.; Harrington, E.; Pallais, A.
title: The Power of Proximity to Coworkers
note: Difference-in-differences study of software engineers at a Fortune 500 firm (2019-2024) using COVID office closures and later return-to-office mandates as proximity shocks. Sitting near teammates raises online feedback on code by roughly 18% and improves code quality, with gains concentrated among junior and less-tenured engineers, while senior engineers write measurably less code when co-located — i.e., mentoring is a real capacity cost borne by the experienced stock. This is the cleanest available quantification of the senior-mentoring-capacity/junior-development tradeoff that the system dynamics model must represent, and it is set in exactly the occupation most exposed to generative AI coding tools.
evidence: Oxford Academic article page academic.oup.com/qje/article/141/3/1825/8676722 giving vol. 141, issue 3, August 2026, pp. 1825-1870, plus the OUP advance-article record carrying DOI 10.1093/qje/qjag027; independently corroborated by the NBER working paper page (w31880), Amanda Pallais's Harvard faculty publications page, and Emma Harrington's 'Published and Accepted Articles' listing. Caveat on title: OUP's HTML renders it as 'Power of Proximity to Coworkers' (and one advance-article page carries an uncorrected typo, 'Coworkres'); NBER, SSRN and both authors' own pages use 'The Power of Proximity to Coworkers', which is the form given here.

authors: Emanuel, N.; Harrington, E.; Pallais, A.
title: The Power of Proximity to Coworkers
note: Quasi-experimental evidence (2020 office closures and 2022-2023 return-to-office mandates) on software engineers at a Fortune 500 firm, 2019-2024. Physical proximity to teammates raises online code feedback received by junior engineers by roughly 18-22% and improves code quality, with gains concentrated among less-tenured and younger engineers building human capital; the same proximity REDUCES the programming output of senior engineers who supply the mentoring. This is the cleanest available quantification of the core tradeoff in a mentoring-capacity stock-and-flow model: senior time is a rival input, so every unit of junior training is paid for in current senior output, and the burden falls disproportionately on women, who both give and receive more mentoring. Directly parameterizes the 'mentoring capacity' constraint and the short-run-output-vs-long-run-pipeline feedback loop.
evidence: Oxford Academic article page academic.oup.com/qje/article/141/3/1825/8676722 (volume 141, issue 3, start page 1825) and the DOI resolver doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjag027; corroborated by NBER Working Paper 31880 (nber.org/papers/w31880), Amanda Pallais's Harvard Scholars publications page, and Emma Harrington's 'Published and Accepted Articles' page. Note: the OUP title field renders as 'Power of Proximity to Coworkers*' (asterisk = acknowledgment footnote; one OUP advance-article listing carries a typo, 'Coworkres'); NBER and both author pages give the canonical form 'The Power of Proximity to Coworkers'. The working-paper subtitle 'Training for Tomorrow or Productivity Today?' was dropped in the published version.

title: People Management Skills, Employee Attrition, and Manager Rewards: An Empirical Analysis
note: Personnel data from a large high-tech firm linking survey-measured people-management skill of supervisors to subordinate outcomes, with identification from newly hired workers and from workers who switch managers. Better people managers substantially reduce subordinate attrition, but do not consistently improve most other observed (non-attrition) outcomes; nevertheless they receive higher subjective performance ratings, faster promotions, and larger raises. Two uses for the model: (i) supervisor quality is a real determinant of whether juniors stay long enough to become experienced, so it is a lever on the junior-to-senior conversion rate; (ii) the reward asymmetry supplies a behavioral micro-foundation for why firms under-invest in developmental supervision relative to the social optimum, motivating policy levers that re-price manager incentives.
evidence: University of Chicago Press journal page journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/711409 (Journal of Political Economy Vol. 129, No. 1); NBER Working Paper 24360 (nber.org/papers/w24360); EconPapers/RePEc record RePEc:ucp:jpolec:doi:10.1086/711409; Semantic Scholar and University of Toronto institutional repository (utoronto.scholaris.ca) records. Volume 129(1), pp. 243-285 confirmed on both the UChicago Press page and the RePEc/EconPapers listing.

title: Managers and Productivity in the Public Sector
note: Italian social security administration data with an output-based productivity measure, identified off the quasi-random rotation of managers across local offices. A one-standard-deviation increase in managerial talent raises office productivity by about 10%; reallocating better managers to the largest and most productive offices would raise output by at least 6.9%. Notably, the gains operate largely through workforce composition (exit/retirement of low-productivity older workers) rather than through raising incumbent effort. Useful in the model as (a) a credible effect size for the managerial-capacity multiplier on team output in a non-experimental, large-scale setting, and (b) a caution that manager effects can run through composition and turnover channels rather than pure skill transfer, which matters for correctly specifying the mentoring-to-human-capital link versus the selection link.
evidence: Econometric Society official publication page (econometricsociety.org, Econometrica Volume 90, Issue 3, May 2022, plus the posted online-appendix supplement ecta200431-sup-0001) and Wiley Online Library onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.3982/ECTA19244; further corroborated by the Econometric Society's 'Volume 90, Issue 3 (May 2022) is now online' announcement, IDEAS/RePEc series listing, and Alessandra Fenizia's faculty research page. Pages 1063-1084 and issue 3 confirmed from the Econometric Society issue listing and Wiley record.

title: Return on investment of apprenticeship systems for enterprises: Evidence from cost-benefit analyses
note: Core reference on the firm-level economics of apprenticeship training: synthesizes cost-benefit survey evidence showing apprentices' productive contribution can offset training costs within the training period (Switzerland, net benefit), whereas German firms bear substantial net costs and must recoup them post-training through retention. Supplies the two competing firm rationales — the 'production' motive versus the 'investment' motive — that a system dynamics model needs to represent why firms hire and train juniors at all, and why the investment channel collapses when expected retention or productive contribution falls (as with genAI substituting for entry-level output).
evidence: Confirmed independently by (a) SpringerLink article page for DOI 10.1186/2193-9004-3-25 in IZA Journal of Labor Policy; (b) IDEAS/RePEc record spr:izalpo:v:3:y:2014:i:1:p:1-22 and the matching EconPapers record, both listing volume 3, issue 1, pages 1-22, article 25; (c) EconStor full text (handle 10419/154697) and the University of Bern BORIS repository record (boris.unibe.ch/65235). Metadata agree across all sources.

authors: Muehlemann, S.; Pfeifer, H.; Wittek, B.H.
title: The effect of business cycle expectations on the German apprenticeship market: Estimating the impact of Covid-19
journal: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
note: Shows empirically that firms' expectations about future business conditions — not just current conditions — drive the decision to open apprenticeship positions, because apprenticeships are partly an investment in filling future skilled-worker slots. Directly supplies the expectations-driven feedback loop for the model: when firms expect reduced future need for (or reduced future value of) junior-trained labour, entry-level training slots contract immediately, ahead of any realized demand change. Uses German state- and occupation-level apprenticeship data 2007-2019 to quantify the elasticity and then project the Covid-19 shock.
evidence: Confirmed independently by (a) SpringerLink article page for DOI 10.1186/s40461-020-00094-9, listing Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training, volume 12, article 8 (2020); (b) PubMed Central record PMC7498563 with the same title, authors and DOI; (c) Crossref Crossmark dialog for the same DOI; (d) the earlier working-paper versions at IZA (Discussion Paper 13368), SSRN (abstract 3628243) and IDEAS/RePEc (unm:umaror:2020008), all with identical authorship and title.

title: Beyond windfall gains: The redistribution of apprenticeship costs and vocational education of care workers
note: Recent quasi-experimental policy evaluation exploiting the staggered introduction of an apprenticeship levy across German federal states in the care sector, which redistributed training costs from training to non-training firms. Finds the cost redistribution raised the probability of hiring new apprentices and the number of apprentices in ambulatory care, with inpatient facilities responding only at the intensive margin. This is the strongest recent evidence for the policy arm of the paper: levy/subsidy schemes that shift net training costs are an effective lever for restoring firm incentives to train juniors when private returns to training are too low.
evidence: Confirmed independently by (a) Wiley Online Library article page for DOI 10.1111/ecca.12474 in Economica (2023); (b) IDEAS/RePEc record bla:econom:v:90:y:2023:i:359:p:978-1002 giving volume 90, issue 359, pages 978-1002. Both sources agree on author (Eric Schuss), title, year and journal; volume/issue/pages taken from the RePEc record and consistent with the Wiley listing.

title: The Persistent Effects of Initial Labor Market Conditions for Young Adults and Their Sources
note: Authoritative survey of the cohort-entry scarring literature: entering the labor market in a downturn produces large initial losses in earnings, wages and labor supply that fade only after 10-15 years, transmitted through downgraded occupations, smaller/lower-paying employers and altered job mobility, with persistent spillovers to fertility, marriage, crime, health and mid-life mortality. Directly supports modeling entry-level hiring collapse as a durable cohort-level stock effect rather than a transient flow disturbance.
evidence: Confirmed independently by the American Economic Association article page (aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jep.34.4.168), the RePEc/EconPapers record (aea/jecper v.34 y.2020 i.4 p.168-94), JSTOR stable/26940895, and the author's UCLA-hosted accepted manuscript (econ.ucla.edu/tvwachter/papers/von_Wachter_JEP_final.pdf). Note: the true title is '...for Young Adults and Their Sources', not '...on Young Adult Outcomes'.

title: The Scars of Youth: Effects of Early-Career Unemployment on Future Unemployment Experience
note: German administrative matched employer-employee data on nearly 700,000 individuals over 24 years, instrumenting early-career unemployment with firm-specific labor demand shocks: each extra day of unemployment in the first eight years of a career raises unemployment over the following 16 years by roughly half a day, with quantile estimates showing far stronger scarring for those already experiencing long or repeated spells. Provides the causal state-dependence coefficient for a reinforcing 'early idleness begets later idleness' feedback loop.
evidence: Confirmed independently by Wiley Online Library (onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/ilr.12079), the IDEAS/RePEc journal record (bla/intlab/v156y2017i3-4p465-494), the Google Scholar lookup entry (volume 156, pages 465-494), Semantic Scholar, and the ILO Research Repository (French-language version). Earlier IAB Discussion Paper 06/2013 version also located on RePEc.

title: The Lost Generation? Labor Market Outcomes for Post-Great Recession Entrants
note: Cohort analysis of US college graduates around the Great Recession: adverse entry conditions permanently depress employment probabilities while medium-term wage scarring fades by the early 30s, but scarring alone cannot explain the collapse in graduate employment, which shows a structural break beginning with the ~2005 entry cohort that has not reversed. Crucial nuance for the paper's argument: a persistent structural downshift in entry-level absorption is distinguishable from, and more damaging than, ordinary cyclical scarring.
evidence: Confirmed independently by the Journal of Human Resources publisher page (jhr.uwpress.org/content/58/5/1452), the IDEAS/RePEc journal record (uwp/jhriss/v58y2023i5p1452-1479), NBER Working Paper 27516, and Harvard Dataverse replication package (doi:10.7910/DVN/SIITYW). A corrigendum by the same author appears in Journal of Human Resources 2025, 60(4), 1458-1467.

title: Unemployment Scarring Effects: An Overview and Meta-Analysis of Empirical Studies
journal: Italian Economic Journal: A Continuation of Rivista Italiana degli Economisti and Giornale degli Economisti
note: Systematic review plus meta-regression of the empirical unemployment-scarring literature, finding homogeneous evidence of significant and often persistent wage losses and strong unemployment state dependence, with effect sizes larger for men and for studies identifying off selection-on-observables. Supplies pooled, publication-bias-adjusted parameter ranges for calibrating the scarring/state-dependence feedback in a system dynamics model rather than relying on any single study's estimate.
evidence: Confirmed independently by the Springer Nature article page (link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40797-023-00228-4), the IDEAS/RePEc journal record (spr/italej/v10y2024i2d10.1007_s40797-023-00228-4, giving vol. 10(2), pp. 459-518, July 2024), Semantic Scholar, and the author's own research page.

title: Global Employment Trends for Youth 2024: Decent Work, Brighter Futures
note: Twelfth edition (20th-anniversary) of the ILO flagship youth labour-market report; documents that global youth unemployment fell to a 15-year low of 13.0% (64.9 million) in 2023 while the NEET share remained stubbornly high, and stresses that the post-COVID recovery in youth employment was uneven across regions. Provides the baseline stock-and-flow data (youth employment, unemployment, NEET) for calibrating the entry-level inflow to the junior-worker stock, and its policy chapter supplies the menu of youth job-creation and school-to-work-transition interventions the model can test.
evidence: ILO Research Repository record (researchrepository.ilo.org/esploro/outputs/report/995379092302676) with the full title 'Global employment trends for youth 2024: decent work, brighter futures'; official ILO full-text PDF at ilo.org/sites/default/files/2024-09/GET_2024_EN%20web.pdf and the executive summary PDF; independently indexed by the ICSF Digital Repository (icsfarchives.net/20325) and ResearchGate, with ISBN 978-92-2040-675-5 reported consistently.

title: OECD Employment Outlook 2025: Can We Get Through the Demographic Crunch?
note: Annual OECD flagship labour-market outlook, published 9 July 2025, focused on population ageing and intergenerational inequality. Directly on point for the paper's mechanism: it reports that young people bear the brunt of current intergenerational disparities and face potential competition with AI for entry-level jobs, and that more than 15% of youth are NEET in nine OECD countries (Colombia, Costa Rica, Greece, Italy, Korea, Lithuania, Mexico, Spain, Turkiye). Its recommendations on cutting school dropout, second-chance education and school-to-work transition support map onto the model's policy levers.
evidence: Official OECD publication landing page (oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-employment-outlook-2025_194a947b-en.html) plus separate OECD full-report component pages for the editorial ('From job shortage to labour shortage: The new challenge of population ageing'), the executive summary, and the 'Setting the scene: Demographic change, economic growth and intergenerational inequalities' chapter; subtitle and framing independently corroborated by the European Commission Digital Skills and Jobs Platform news item 'OECD Employment Outlook 2025: can we get through the demographic crunch?'

title: NEET youth in central and eastern European countries: a panel model approach
note: Fixed-effects panel analysis of the macro-determinants of the NEET rate across 16 Central and Eastern European countries, 2013-2021, using Eurostat, UNESCO and World Bank data. Tests early school leaving, VET enrolment, unemployment, labour-market regulation, GDP, education expenditure and the human development index as drivers of NEET. Useful as an empirically estimated set of causal links and elasticities for the NEET/disengagement sector of the system dynamics model, and as evidence that VET enrolment and education spending are effective policy levers.
evidence: Taylor & Francis Online article record listing it under Journal of Youth Studies Vol. 28, No. 9 (tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13676261.2024.2392189) and the earlier online-first abstract record (doi/abs, 'Vol 0, No 0', published online 20 August 2024); author identity and affiliation (Emiljan Karma, Research Centre on Economies of Transition Countries, Catholic University Our Lady of Good Counsel, Tirana, Albania) corroborated by the Acume researcher profile, with volume/issue/page range 1458-1475 returned consistently across independent queries.

authors: Budzyń, K.; Romańczyk, M.; Kitala, D.; Kołodziej, P.; Bugajski, M.; Adami, H.-O.; Blom, J.; Buszkiewicz, M.; Halvorsen, N.G.; Hassan, C.; et al.
title: Endoscopist deskilling risk after exposure to artificial intelligence in colonoscopy: a multicentre, observational study
note: Retrospective multicentre study of four Polish endoscopy centres in the ACCEPT trial: after routine introduction of AI polyp detection, the adenoma detection rate of standard NON-AI-assisted colonoscopy fell from 28.4% to 22.4% (a 6.0 percentage-point absolute decline). First real-world evidence of automation-induced deskilling in a professional task with direct patient-outcome consequences; the canonical empirical anchor for a skill-atrophy feedback loop in a system dynamics model. Note: a correction (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025) added an omitted covariate to the multivariable analysis without changing the interpretation.
evidence: thelancet.com article page (PIIS2468-1253(25)00133-5); ScienceDirect record S2468125325001335; Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology commentary (s41575-025-01122-3); University of Oslo Institute of Health and Society news release; EurekAlert press release; SSRN preprint listing full author roster; Lancet correction notice citing 'Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025; 10: 896-903'

authors: Klingbeil, A.; Grützner, C.; Schreck, P.
title: Trust and reliance on AI — An experimental study on the extent and costs of overreliance on AI
note: Incentivized, interactive, domain-independent behavioural experiment showing that the mere knowledge that advice was AI-generated causes people to overrely on it — following AI advice even when it contradicts available contextual information and their own assessment. Also documents downstream costs: overreliance degrades human cooperation and imposes losses on advisees and third parties. Direct evidence that the 'human verifies the AI' step is far weaker in practice than models assume.
evidence: ScienceDirect S0747563224002206; ACM Digital Library record for 10.1016/j.chb.2024.108352; Semantic Scholar entry (Klingbeil-Grützner); SCIRP reference record giving volume 160, article 108352; Google Scholar citation lookup with matching volume/pages; dblp author page for Artur Klingbeil (Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg)

authors: Vaccaro, M.; Almaatouq, A.; Malone, T.
title: When combinations of humans and AI are useful: A systematic review and meta-analysis
note: Preregistered meta-analysis of 106 experimental studies and 370 effect sizes: on average human-AI combinations performed significantly WORSE than the better of human alone or AI alone. Losses concentrated in decision-making tasks, gains in content creation; losses were largest precisely where the AI already outperformed the human. Quantitative justification for treating human-in-the-loop oversight as a costly, capacity-limited, and often value-subtracting stage rather than a free safety net.
evidence: nature.com article s41562-024-02024-1; PubMed 39468277; Semantic Scholar record; arXiv:2405.06087 preprint; SCIRP reference record giving 8, 2293-2303; MIT Sloan press release

authors: Qin, X.; Zhou, X.; Chen, C.; Wu, D.; Zhou, H.; Dong, X.; Cao, L.; Lu, J.G.
title: AI Aversion or Appreciation? A Capability–Personalization Framework and a Meta-Analytic Review
note: Meta-analysis of 442 effect sizes from 163 studies (N = 82,078) resolving the algorithm-aversion vs. algorithm-appreciation contradiction: appreciation (d = 0.27) emerges when AI is perceived as more capable and the task is perceived as not requiring personalization; aversion emerges otherwise. Moderators include country-level education, internet use, and unemployment. Gives an empirically grounded, task-contingent adoption-propensity parameter for modelling where firms substitute AI for junior labour and where they do not.
evidence: APA/Ovid abstract page for 10.1037/bul0000477 giving vol. 151(5), 580-599; APA supplemental materials page (bul0000477_supp); Semantic Scholar record (Qin-Zhou); Sun Yat-sen University Business School hosted PDF ('PB, 2025, AI Aversion or Appreciation'); MIT Sloan press release; EurekAlert release

authors: Fügener, A.; Grahl, J.; Gupta, A.; Ketter, W.
title: Cognitive Challenges in Human–Artificial Intelligence Collaboration: Investigating the Path Toward Productive Delegation
note: Experimental study of delegation in human-AI classification teams. Human-AI teams beat AI alone only when the AI delegates to the human, not when the human delegates to the AI, because humans lack the metaknowledge to assess their own competence relative to the machine. Slightly outside the 2023-2026 window but the cleanest evidence for a 'human-in-the-loop capacity constraint': oversight quality is bounded by workers' inaccurate self-assessment, which worsens as juniors accumulate less independent experience.
evidence: INFORMS PubsOnLine article and PDF for 10.1287/isre.2021.1079; RePEc/EconPapers record inmorisre v:33 y:2022 i:2 p:678-696; Erasmus University Rotterdam Pure repository; Experts@Minnesota repository; SSRN working-paper version (abstract 3368813)
